tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, and standard web media types only; one publish sends at most 255 files and 64MB, while a version may hold up to 511 files and 256MB in all, so a larger set goes up over several publishes to the same `url` (each later publish adds to the files already there).

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. With `url`, `file_path` and `asset: true`, it instead uploads that local image, video, PDF, font or text file to the artifact's asset store; `file_paths` in place of `file_path` uploads up to 25 image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in one call under one approval (a text file goes in a call of its own), and the result gives each one's `url`. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# =============================================================================
3	# Nxeon — onboard a fresh Proxmox VE host as a compute node
4	# =============================================================================
5	# Run this ON the new Proxmox host (as root). It idempotently preps everything a
6	# Nxeon compute node needs, then prints the exact values to paste into the admin
7	# "Add node" form (/admin/nodes/new). Re-running is safe: every step checks
8	# current state before changing anything.
9	#
10	# What it does:
11	#   1. Create a NAT bridge vmbrX bound to a per-node /24 (e.g. 10.20.N.1/24)
12	#   2. Enable IPv4 forwarding + a MASQUERADE rule for that subnet (append-only)
13	#   3. Create the NVMe + HDD storages matching the Node's storageNvme/storageHdd
14	#   4. Create the cloud-init snippets dir + the nxeon vendor snippet
15	#   5. Create a Proxmox API role + user + token with the privileges the platform
16	#      needs (documented pveum commands)
17	#   6. Build (or document copying) the cloud-init templates VMID 9000-9004
18	#   7. Print the Add-node form values (apiUrl, tokenId, tokenSecret, pveNode,
19	#      subnetPrefix, natChain, sshPort range, storages, publicIp)
20	#
21	# SAFETY:
22	#   - Never flushes the firewall. It only APPENDS its own MASQUERADE/FORWARD
23	#     rules and only if an identical rule is not already present.
24	#   - Never touches running VMs. Template builds skip any VMID that exists.
25	#   - Never destroys storage. `pvesm add` is skipped when the storage id exists.
26	#
27	# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
28	# CROSS-HOST NETWORKING — IMPORTANT LIMITATION (read before deploying node #2)
29	# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
30	# Each node NATs its OWN private /24 (10.20.N.0/24) behind its OWN public IP.
31	# This makes each node fully self-sufficient for provisioning, IP allocation and
32	# SSH DNAT — but it does NOT give VMs on different physical hosts a shared LAN.
33	#
34	#   * A VM on node-1 (10.20.0.x) CANNOT reach a VM on node-2 (10.20.1.x) over the
35	#     private network. They are separate NAT islands.
36	#   * The worker's iptables NAT chain (NXEON_FWD*) is rebuilt per-host from the
37	#     DB; it only manages forwards local to the host it runs on.
38	#
39	# If you need private east-west connectivity between VMs on different nodes you
40	# must lay an overlay/VPN over the public IPs — e.g. WireGuard mesh or a VXLAN
41	# fabric (Proxmox SDN "VXLAN zone") — and route the /24s across it. That is out
42	# of scope for this script; it is a deliberate, documented follow-up. For the
43	# common case (independent single-node VPS customers) per-node NAT islands are
44	# exactly what you want.
45	#
46	# Assumption: node #2 is a SEPARATE physical box with its own public IP, NOT a
47	# second NIC on the same L2 as node #1. If two nodes truly share L2 you would
48	# instead give them the SAME bridge/subnet and split the IP range — but this
49	# script assumes the separate-host model above.
50	# =============================================================================
51	set -euo pipefail
52	
53	# ---------- Parameters (flags override env) ----------------------------------
54	NODE_NUM="${NODE_NUM:-2}"           # ordinal; drives subnet + nat chain defaults
55	SUBNET_OCTET=""                     # third octet of 10.20.X.0/24 (default: NODE_NUM-1)
56	PUBLIC_IP="${PUBLIC_IP:-}"          # this host's public IPv4 (auto-detected if empty)
57	BRIDGE=""                           # vmbrX (default: vmbr1)
58	NVME_STORAGE="${NVME_STORAGE:-vmdata}"
59	HDD_STORAGE="${HDD_STORAGE:-vmdata-hdd}"
60	NVME_ZPOOL="${NVME_ZPOOL:-}"        # existing ZFS pool for NVMe storage (optional)
61	HDD_DIR="${HDD_DIR:-/tank/backup}"  # dir-backed HDD storage path
62	SNIPPETS_STORAGE="${SNIPPETS_STORAGE:-$HDD_STORAGE}"
63	TOKEN_USER="${TOKEN_USER:-nxeon@pve}"
64	TOKEN_NAME="${TOKEN_NAME:-platform}"
65	TOKEN_ROLE="${TOKEN_ROLE:-NxeonProvision}"
66	BUILD_TEMPLATES="${BUILD_TEMPLATES:-0}"   # 1 = build 9000-9004 here; 0 = document copying
67	SSH_PORT_START="${SSH_PORT_START:-20000}"
68	SSH_PORT_END="${SSH_PORT_END:-29999}"
69	PRIMARY_IP="${PRIMARY_IP:-}"          # the PRIMARY node's own public IP — required for the firewall + agent-allow steps
70	AGENT_PORT="${AGENT_PORT:-8943}"      # must match the value later entered in the admin "Add node" form
71	SKIP_FIREWALL="${SKIP_FIREWALL:-0}"
72	SKIP_AGENT="${SKIP_AGENT:-0}"
73	SKIP_BACKUPS="${SKIP_BACKUPS:-0}"
74	ARC_MAX_GB="${ARC_MAX_GB:-8}"          # ZFS ARC cap — matches the primary/node-3 precedent; see step 4
75	
76	usage() {
77	  cat <<EOF
78	Usage: $0 [flags]
79	  --node-num N          Node ordinal (default 2). Sets defaults for subnet + nat chain.
80	  --subnet-octet N      Third octet of the /24 (default: node-num - 1, e.g. node 2 -> 1 -> 10.20.1.0/24).
81	  --public-ip IP        This host's public IPv4 (auto-detected if omitted).
82	  --bridge vmbrX        NAT bridge name (default vmbr1).
83	  --nvme-storage NAME   NVMe storage id (default vmdata).
84	  --hdd-storage NAME    HDD storage id (default vmdata-hdd).
85	  --nvme-zpool POOL     Existing ZFS pool to back the NVMe storage (zfspool). Optional.
86	  --hdd-dir PATH        Directory for the HDD (dir) storage (default /tank/backup).
87	  --build-templates     Build cloud-init templates 9000-9004 on this host.
88	  --primary-ip IP       The PRIMARY node's own public IP (required unless --skip-firewall
89	                         AND --skip-agent are both given — it's the only address ever
90	                         allowed to reach this node's admin ports / node-agent port).
91	  --agent-port N        Port the node-agent listens on (default 8943; must match what you
92	                         enter in the admin "Add node" form).
93	  --skip-firewall       Don't touch this host's firewall (do it yourself, or later).
94	  --skip-agent          Don't install the node-agent (do it yourself, or later).
95	  --skip-backups        Don't install this node's own local disaster-recovery backups.
96	  --arc-max-gb N        ZFS ARC cap in GB (default 8 — matches the primary/node-3 precedent).
97	  -h, --help            Show this help.
98	
99	Environment variables mirror the flags (NODE_NUM, PUBLIC_IP, BRIDGE, PRIMARY_IP, ...).
100	
101	PREREQUISITE for --primary-ip's firewall/agent steps: this script expects the following
102	files to already sit alongside it (e.g. clone/copy the whole repo, or just these paths,
103	onto this host before running):
104	  scripts/firewall-node.nft, scripts/admin-ip.sh, scripts/firewall-safe-apply.sh,
105	  scripts/firewall-reachability.sh, deploy/fail2ban-nxeon.jail.conf,
106	  deploy/nxeon-firewall.service, node-agent/index.js, deploy/nxeon-node-agent.service,
107	  scripts/backup-vms.sh, scripts/backup-pve-config.sh, deploy/nxeon-backup-vms.service,
108	  deploy/nxeon-backup-vms.timer
109	Missing files are reported and that step is skipped (never blocks the rest of onboarding).
110	EOF
111	}
112	
113	while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
114	  case "$1" in
115	    --node-num) NODE_NUM="$2"; shift 2 ;;
116	    --subnet-octet) SUBNET_OCTET="$2"; shift 2 ;;
117	    --public-ip) PUBLIC_IP="$2"; shift 2 ;;
118	    --bridge) BRIDGE="$2"; shift 2 ;;
119	    --nvme-storage) NVME_STORAGE="$2"; shift 2 ;;
120	    --hdd-storage) HDD_STORAGE="$2"; shift 2 ;;
121	    --nvme-zpool) NVME_ZPOOL="$2"; shift 2 ;;
122	    --hdd-dir) HDD_DIR="$2"; shift 2 ;;
123	    --build-templates) BUILD_TEMPLATES=1; shift ;;
124	    --primary-ip) PRIMARY_IP="$2"; shift 2 ;;
125	    --agent-port) AGENT_PORT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
126	    --skip-firewall) SKIP_FIREWALL=1; shift ;;
127	    --skip-agent) SKIP_AGENT=1; shift ;;
128	    --skip-backups) SKIP_BACKUPS=1; shift ;;
129	    --arc-max-gb) ARC_MAX_GB="$2"; shift 2 ;;
130	    -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
131	    *) echo "Unknown flag: $1" >&2; usage; exit 1 ;;
132	  esac
133	done
134	
135	# ---------- Derived values ---------------------------------------------------
136	[[ -z "$SUBNET_OCTET" ]] && SUBNET_OCTET="$((NODE_NUM - 1))"
137	[[ -z "$BRIDGE" ]] && BRIDGE="vmbr1"
138	SUBNET_PREFIX="10.20.${SUBNET_OCTET}."
139	SUBNET_CIDR="10.20.${SUBNET_OCTET}.0/24"
140	GATEWAY_IP="10.20.${SUBNET_OCTET}.1"
141	if [[ "$NODE_NUM" -le 1 ]]; then
142	  NAT_CHAIN="NXEON_FWD"
143	else
144	  NAT_CHAIN="NXEON_FWD_N${NODE_NUM}"
145	fi
146	PVE_NODE="$(hostname)"
147	[[ -z "$PUBLIC_IP" ]] && PUBLIC_IP="$(hostname -I 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')"
148	SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
149	REPO_DIR="$(cd "${SCRIPT_DIR}/.." && pwd)"
150	
151	log()  { echo -e "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] $*"; }
152	ok()   { echo -e "  \033[32m✓\033[0m $*"; }
153	warn() { echo -e "  \033[33m!\033[0m $*"; }
154	
155	require_root() { [[ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]] || { echo "Run as root on the Proxmox host." >&2; exit 1; }; }
156	require_cmd()  { command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing required command: $1" >&2; exit 1; }; }
157	
158	require_root
159	require_cmd pvesm
160	require_cmd pveum
161	require_cmd iptables
162	
163	log "Onboarding node #${NODE_NUM} — ${PVE_NODE} (${PUBLIC_IP})"
164	log "  subnet ${SUBNET_CIDR} via ${BRIDGE} (gw ${GATEWAY_IP}), NAT chain ${NAT_CHAIN}"
165	
166	# =============================================================================
167	# 1 + 2. NAT bridge + ip_forward + MASQUERADE
168	# =============================================================================
169	log "[1/11] NAT bridge ${BRIDGE} (${GATEWAY_IP}/24)"
170	if ip link show "$BRIDGE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
171	  ok "bridge ${BRIDGE} already exists — leaving it as-is"
172	else
173	  # Append an isolated (no physical port) NAT bridge to /etc/network/interfaces.
174	  # We do NOT reload all interfaces (that could disrupt the host); we bring up
175	  # just this bridge with ifup.
176	  if ! grep -qE "^\s*auto\s+${BRIDGE}\b" /etc/network/interfaces 2>/dev/null; then
177	    cat >>/etc/network/interfaces <<EOF
178	
179	# --- Nxeon node #${NODE_NUM} NAT bridge (added by onboard-node.sh) ---
180	auto ${BRIDGE}
181	iface ${BRIDGE} inet static
182	        address ${GATEWAY_IP}/24
183	        bridge-ports none
184	        bridge-stp off
185	        bridge-fd 0
186	        post-up   echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
187	        post-up   iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s ${SUBNET_CIDR} ! -d ${SUBNET_CIDR} -j MASQUERADE
188	        post-down iptables -t nat -D POSTROUTING -s ${SUBNET_CIDR} ! -d ${SUBNET_CIDR} -j MASQUERADE
189	EOF
190	    ok "wrote ${BRIDGE} stanza to /etc/network/interfaces"
191	  fi
192	  ifup "$BRIDGE" 2>/dev/null || warn "ifup ${BRIDGE} failed — bring it up manually / on next reboot"
193	  ip link show "$BRIDGE" >/dev/null 2>&1 && ok "bridge ${BRIDGE} is up"
194	fi
195	
196	log "[2/11] IPv4 forwarding + MASQUERADE (append-only, never flush)"
197	# Persist ip_forward.
198	if ! sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward 2>/dev/null | grep -q ' = 1'; then
199	  sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 >/dev/null

317	# 5. Proxmox API role + user + token
318	# =============================================================================
319	log "[6/11] Proxmox API role/user/token (${TOKEN_USER}!${TOKEN_NAME})"
320	# Role privileges: everything the worker/web need to clone, configure, run and
321	# monitor VMs, allocate cloud-init, and read node/storage status. Mirrors the
322	# privileges of the primary node's platform token.
323	#
324	# VM.GuestAgent.Audit is REQUIRED for in-guest disk sampling: the monitor calls
325	# the qemu guest-agent's get-fsinfo (worker/monitor.ts sampleServerDisks), which
326	# Proxmox gates behind this privilege. Without it get-fsinfo returns 403 and the
327	# panel's disk-usage figures never populate.
328	#
329	# VM.Backup is REQUIRED for BACKUP_CREATE: vzdump 403s ("Permission check failed
330	# (/vms/N, VM.Backup)") without it, so the paid/auto-backup feature is dead
331	# fleet-wide. Learned the hard way — it was missing from the original role.
332	#
333	# NB: do NOT add VM.Monitor here — it was removed in Proxmox VE 9 and `pveum role
334	# modify` rejects the whole call with "invalid privilege 'VM.Monitor'" (400),
335	# leaving the role unchanged. The privilege names below are validated against the
336	# built-in Administrator role on a PVE 9 host.
337	# SDN.Use is REQUIRED on Proxmox VE 9: attaching a VM NIC to a bridge — even the
338	# default localnetwork zone / vmbr1 — is now permission-checked under
339	# /sdn/zones/localnetwork/<bridge>. Without it, any clone/config that sets net0
340	# fails with "Permission check failed (/sdn/zones/localnetwork/vmbr1, SDN.Use)",
341	# which silently broke reinstall/provision on PVE9 (the VM is destroyed, then the
342	# re-clone can't run).
343	ROLE_PRIVS="VM.Allocate,VM.Clone,VM.Config.Disk,VM.Config.CPU,VM.Config.Memory,VM.Config.Network,VM.Config.Options,VM.Config.CDROM,VM.Config.Cloudinit,VM.Config.HWType,VM.PowerMgmt,VM.Backup,VM.Audit,VM.Console,VM.Snapshot,VM.Snapshot.Rollback,VM.GuestAgent.Audit,SDN.Use,Datastore.Allocate,Datastore.AllocateSpace,Datastore.AllocateTemplate,Datastore.Audit,Sys.Audit,Sys.Console,Sys.Modify,Pool.Allocate"
344	
345	# --output-format json + python3, not the human-readable box-table: that
346	# table wraps/pads at a detected terminal width, and a non-interactive SSH
347	# run (no real tty) can get a width where `grep -w` no longer matches a role
348	# already present — confirmed live re-running this script against node-2
349	# minutes after its first, successful run: the role genuinely existed, this
350	# check said it didn't, and `pveum role add` then failed loudly enough
351	# (under `set -e`) to abort the rest of onboarding.
352	role_exists() { pveum role list --output-format json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
353	import json, sys
354	try:
355	    roles = json.load(sys.stdin)
356	except Exception:
357	    sys.exit(1)
358	sys.exit(0 if any(r.get('roleid') == '$1' for r in roles) else 1)
359	"; }
360	user_exists() { pveum user list --output-format json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
361	import json, sys
362	try:
363	    users = json.load(sys.stdin)
364	except Exception:
365	    sys.exit(1)
366	sys.exit(0 if any(u.get('userid') == '$1' for u in users) else 1)
367	"; }
368	
369	if role_exists "$TOKEN_ROLE"; then
370	  ok "role ${TOKEN_ROLE} exists — updating privileges"
371	  pveum role modify "$TOKEN_ROLE" --privs "$ROLE_PRIVS"
372	else
373	  pveum role add "$TOKEN_ROLE" --privs "$ROLE_PRIVS"
374	  ok "created role ${TOKEN_ROLE}"
375	fi
376	
377	# User (realm@pve). Create if missing.
378	if user_exists "$TOKEN_USER"; then
379	  ok "user ${TOKEN_USER} exists"
380	else
381	  pveum user add "$TOKEN_USER"
382	  ok "created user ${TOKEN_USER}"
383	fi
384	
385	# Grant the role at / (propagating). Idempotent — re-running is harmless.
386	pveum acl modify / --users "$TOKEN_USER" --roles "$TOKEN_ROLE" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
387	ok "granted ${TOKEN_ROLE} to ${TOKEN_USER} at / (propagate)"
388	
389	# Token. If it already exists we cannot re-read the secret (Proxmox only shows it
390	# once at creation), so we leave it and tell the operator to reuse the stored one
391	# or delete+recreate. Same JSON-based check as role_exists/user_exists above —
392	# `pveum user token add` on an existing token name fails outright (Proxmox
393	# does not silently rotate on add), so the fragile table-grep version of this
394	# check was "only" ever going to print a confusing wrong warning here, not
395	# actually invalidate a live token — still worth the same fix for clarity.
396	token_exists() { pveum user token list "$1" --output-format json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
397	import json, sys
398	try:
399	    tokens = json.load(sys.stdin)
400	except Exception:
401	    sys.exit(1)
402	sys.exit(0 if any(t.get('tokenid') == '$2' for t in tokens) else 1)
403	"; }
404	TOKEN_SECRET=""
405	if token_exists "$TOKEN_USER" "$TOKEN_NAME"; then
406	  warn "token ${TOKEN_USER}!${TOKEN_NAME} already exists — its secret is only shown once."
407	  warn "  Reuse the secret you saved when it was created, OR rotate it:"
408	  warn "    pveum user token remove ${TOKEN_USER} ${TOKEN_NAME}"
409	  warn "    pveum user token add ${TOKEN_USER} ${TOKEN_NAME} --privsep 0"
410	else
411	  # --privsep 0 => token inherits the user's privileges (the role we granted).
412	  TOKEN_OUT="$(pveum user token add "$TOKEN_USER" "$TOKEN_NAME" --privsep 0 2>/dev/null || true)"
413	  TOKEN_SECRET="$(echo "$TOKEN_OUT" | grep -iE 'value|secret' | grep -oE '[0-9a-f-]{36}' | head -n1)"
414	  if [[ -n "$TOKEN_SECRET" ]]; then
415	    ok "created token ${TOKEN_USER}!${TOKEN_NAME}"
416	  else
417	    warn "token created but could not parse the secret from output — run manually:"
418	    warn "  pveum user token add ${TOKEN_USER} ${TOKEN_NAME} --privsep 0"
419	  fi
420	fi

## Multi-node rollout — going from one Proxmox host to two (2026-09-05)

### Motivation and timeline

Nxeon ran on a single Proxmox compute node (the primary, OVH, confirmed via `geoip-lite` against its
live public IP to genuinely be in **Singapore**, not the `bhs`/Canada guess an env-var default had
suggested — always verify a datacenter claim against the live IP, never trust an inferred default) from
launch until 2026-09-05, when a Hetzner server auction listing (#3068915 — i7-8700, 64GB RAM, 2×476.9GB
NVMe, 1×1.92TB SATA SSD, Falkenstein/Germany, one included IPv4 + a routed IPv6 /64) was purchased to
start a European presence. Same day: schema + admin dashboards generalized for multiple nodes, the
physical box installed and onboarded as `node-2`, then a full platform audit (prompted by the owner
asking "the primary node needs to be able to have complete control of all of the nodes, complete
sync — am I right?") found the rollout needed to go further than "the code runs on two nodes" — see
"What the audit found" below. `node-2` was deliberately kept `enabled: false` in the DB through most of
this work; zero real customers were ever provisioned onto it during the entire rollout.

### Schema changes

- `enum NodeProvider { OVH HETZNER }` — a real enum (unlike `Node.region`, a validated plain string —
  see `lib/node-regions.ts`'s `NODE_REGIONS`/`REGION_LABELS`/`REGION_COUNTRY`), because a new
  infrastructure provider is a rare, deliberate business event while datacenter codes grow far more
  often, matching this schema's existing convention (`StaffGrant.area` uses the same "string,
  validated in code" pattern for the same reason).
- `Node.provider`, `Node.region` (default `"sgp1"` for the primary, confirmed Singapore per above),
  `Node.providerServerId` (the provider's own identifier for the box — OVH's "service name" or
  Hetzner's server number — distinct from `pveNode`, needed by the per-node dedicated-IP branch).
- `DedicatedIp.nodeId` (required, FK to `Node`) — added nullable, backfilled every existing row to the
  primary's id, then tightened to `NOT NULL` with the FK constraint, all in one hand-reviewed manual
  migration (`prisma/manual-migrations/2026-09-05-node-provider-region.sql`) rather than two separate
  `db push` rounds — production has real `DedicatedIp` rows, and `prisma db push` cannot auto-populate
  a new required relation column against non-empty data (confirmed live: `promote-production.sh`'s
  usual `db push --accept-data-loss` refused with "you may use --force-reset... all data will be lost"
  on this exact migration, precisely because 9 real rows existed — the manual-migration-file convention
  this repo already uses for schema changes exists for exactly this scenario, and paid off immediately).
- Contrast with `HostingNode` (the separate shared-hosting product's node model): `HostingNode` has
  `sshHost`/`sshPort`/`rootPasswordEnc` because that product's trust model is direct SSH to each box;
  `Node` deliberately has no SSH fields, only a scoped Proxmox API token (`apiUrl`/`tokenId`/
  `tokenSecret`) — a real, deliberate difference in security posture between the two products, not an
  oversight to "fix" by adding SSH fields to `Node`.

### Hetzner API client + dedicated-IP generalization

`lib/hetzner.ts` (new) mirrors `lib/ovh.ts`'s shape but reflects real wire-format differences: HTTP
Basic Auth (not OVH's signed AK/AS/CK headers), form-urlencoded bodies (not JSON), and additional IPs
route straight to the server's real MAC with a **per-IP gateway read from Hetzner's own API response**
(not a fixed `.254`-of-the-/24 formula like OVH, and no "Virtual MAC" object to create/poll/delete).
`hetznerApi.orderAdditionalIp()` is a deliberate stub that throws "not implemented" — the exact Robot
API endpoint for a real, paid IP-ordering transaction could not be confirmed from available
documentation, and this is not something to guess at for an endpoint that spends real money.
`lib/dedicated-ip.ts` was rewritten to resolve a `Node` row and branch by `provider` per call
(`resolveNode`, `dedicatedIpProviderConfigured`, `syncOvhPool`/`syncHetznerPool`) instead of one
hardcoded OVH server constant — additive; every existing importer that never passes a `nodeId` still
resolves to the primary, unchanged.

### Per-server Proxmox correctness fixes (Step 4)

Multiple customer/staff/Discord-bot surfaces called bare Proxmox singleton functions
(`vmStatus`/`listSnapshots`/`listBackups`) bound to the primary's env-derived credentials regardless of
which node a server actually lives on — harmless with one node (nothing to route to *wrong*), a real
"customer sees another tenant's VM stats" bug the instant a second node has real traffic, since vmids
are not globally unique across physical hosts. Fixed in `app/dashboard/servers/[id]/page.tsx`,
`app/admin/servers/[id]/page.tsx`, `lib/discord-status-command.ts`, `app/api/servers/[id]/backups/
download/route.ts`, and `lib/actions-server-ops.ts`, all routing through a new `pveForNode(node)`
helper in `lib/proxmox.ts`. (The much larger, platform-wide version of this same bug class — SSH/RCON
connection resolution, not just Proxmox API calls — is covered under "What the audit found" below; this
Step-4 fix only covered the Proxmox-API half.)

### Admin dashboards + deploy wizard (Steps 5, 7)

`app/admin/monitoring/page.tsx` (VM table + node-metrics chart), `app/admin/page.tsx` (fleet health
summary), and `app/admin/infrastructure/page.tsx` (per-node cards) were redesigned to loop every
enabled `Node` instead of showing only the primary's numbers — `lib/monitoring.ts`'s `nodeTargets()`/
`nodeRamUsage()`/`nodeStorageUsage()` already had the right multi-node shape from earlier work and
needed no changes; the dashboards just needed to actually call them instead of the bare singletons.
Added `nodeStatus`/`listVms`/`storageStatus`/`nodeRrd` optional-`conn` parameters to `lib/proxmox.ts`
(mirroring `vmRrd`'s existing pattern) so these could be called per-node. `components/admin/NodeForms.tsx`,
`app/admin/nodes/page.tsx`/`[id]/page.tsx`, and the customer deploy wizard's location picker
(`components/customer/DeployWizard.tsx`) got Provider/Region fields and badges — the customer-facing
picker deliberately shows only a country flag + region name (`lib/flag-emoji.ts` → later replaced with
an image-based `components/ui/CountryFlag.tsx` once Unicode regional-indicator emoji turned out not to
render as flags on all platforms, notably Windows), never the provider name or raw IP — matching the
standing brand rule that Nxeon never surfaces a third-party infrastructure provider to customers.

### The physical install (kept verbatim from the original entry)

Nxeon's second compute node (`node-2`, Hetzner auction server #3068915, Falkenstein, `nxeon-fsn1`,
178.63.94.114) was onboarded using the standard "install via QEMU inside Hetzner's rescue system"
technique: boot into Hetzner rescue, download the official Proxmox VE ISO, bake an automated-install
`answer.toml` into it with `proxmox-auto-install-assistant`, then boot that ISO under
`qemu-system-x86_64` with the real physical disks passed through directly (`-drive file=/dev/nvme0n1`
etc., emulated as `-device nvme` so the guest sees the same `nvme0n1`/`nvme1n1` names the answer file's
`disk-list` references), so the installer partitions the actual hardware. When it finishes, reboot the
physical host out of rescue mode into the fresh install.

**Real gotcha #1 — the network `filter` must match the EMULATED NIC, not the real one.** The
automated installer's `[network]` answer-file section needs a `filter.ID_NET_NAME_MAC` (or similar) to
pick which NIC to configure. It's tempting to set this to the REAL hardware NIC's MAC (read via
`udevadm info -p /sys/class/net/eth0` in rescue mode beforehand) — but during the QEMU install, the
installer only ever sees QEMU's *emulated* NIC, which has a different MAC unless you explicitly spoof
it. Fix: pass `-netdev user,id=net0 -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=net0,mac=<real-nic-mac>` to `qemu`
so the emulated NIC's MAC matches what the answer file's filter expects. Without this the installer
aborts cleanly with `ERROR: Installation failed: filter did not match any device` — annoying but safe
(no partial install).

**Real gotcha #2 — the real hang: the emulated NIC's INTERFACE NAME leaks into `/etc/network/interfaces`.**
Even after fixing gotcha #1, the resulting install boots to a *completely silent* host — no ping, no
SSH, indefinitely — which looks exactly like a hung/crashed boot. It is not. The installer's network
setup writes the interface name it saw for the matched NIC *at install time* into
`/etc/network/interfaces` (e.g. `auto vmbr0 ... bridge-ports ens5`). Under QEMU, a `virtio-net-pci`
device gets a PCI-Express slot-based name like `ens5` — a name that has nothing to do with the real
hardware's PCI topology. On the real physical box, the same NIC gets whatever systemd-udevd's
predictable-naming scheme actually assigns (onboard index like `eno1` takes priority when the
firmware provides `ID_NET_NAME_ONBOARD`, which `udevadm info` will show ahead of time). Since `ens5`
never exists on the real hardware, the bridge never comes up, and the OS boots completely fine with a
dead network — indistinguishable from a boot hang from the outside.

**Fix, done live via a follow-up rescue-mode session:** reboot into rescue, `apt-get install
zfs-fuse` (this rescue kernel's exact build doesn't have a matching `zfs-dkms` target — `zfs-fuse` is
a userspace ZFS impl that doesn't care) OR use Hetzner's own `/usr/local/sbin/zpool` wrapper, which
offers to compile OpenZFS from source against the *exact* running rescue kernel (works, takes ~1-2
min, answer `y` to the CDDL/GPL notice) — either way, `zpool import -N -f -R /mnt rpool`, `zfs mount`
the root + data datasets, edit `/etc/network/interfaces` to replace the QEMU-era interface name with
the real one, `zpool export rpool`, reboot. Confirmed the real interface name ahead of time via
`udevadm info -p /sys/class/net/<ifname>` while still in the FIRST rescue session (`ID_NET_NAME_ONBOARD`)
so the fix wasn't a guess.

**Lesson for next time:** decide the real interface name from `udevadm` BEFORE running the automated
install, and consider setting the answer file's network filter AND expected interface name to
whatever the real hardware will assign — or simplest, just always plan for this one manual
`/etc/network/interfaces` edit as a normal step of this onboarding method, not an exceptional failure.
Silence (no ping, no SSH) after a QEMU-installed reboot is NOT necessarily a firmware/boot-order
problem — check the installed system's actual network config from rescue mode before assuming
anything about the boot process itself. (A red herring chased first: BIOS boot-order priority hitting
a blank spare disk before the OS disks — real hardware here does default to legacy BIOS, confirmed via
`[ -d /sys/firmware/efi ]` in rescue mode, and cloning the NVMe mirror's GRUB boot code onto the blank
SATA SSD via `dd` was a reasonable, low-risk thing to try, but it was not the actual cause.)

**Template parity:** rather than building fresh cloud-init templates (9000-9004) on the new node,
`vzdump <id> --dumpdir /tank/backup` on the primary for each, `scp` the `.vma` files to the new node's
own `/tank/backup`, then `qmrestore <file> <id> --storage vmdata` — `qmrestore` preserves the
`template: 1` flag from the original config automatically (the "you can't convert a template to a
template" message on a subsequent `qm template <id>` call is expected/harmless, not an error). This
keeps every node's base images byte-identical, matching `scripts/onboard-node.sh`'s own stated
preference over `--build-templates`.

### What the full audit found (2026-09-05)

Enabling `node-2` for real traffic surfaced one confirmed bug (the worker's NAT/port-forward sync only
ever touches the primary's own iptables). Asking "does the primary genuinely have complete control/sync
over every node" turned into a full platform audit (3 parallel deep-research passes + 1 design pass,
all cross-verified against live code and the live host) that found the real picture was much bigger:

- **One shared root-cause function breaks nearly the entire SSH-based control panel for any non-primary
  server.** `lib/sftp.ts`'s `connectionTarget()` resolves a non-dedicated-IP server's SSH host as
  `process.env.PUBLIC_IP` (the primary's address) and never consults `server.node.publicIp` — this one
  function underlies `lib/ssh-exec.ts`'s `withServerSsh()`/`exec()`, which is the shared plumbing for
  the web terminal, file manager, game console/RCON/kick/ban, game power/backup/scheduled-restart/
  player-tracking, the cPanel-lite control panel (websites/DBs/services/one-click apps), SSL issuance,
  game mods/config, the guest-side half of disk-expand/volume-attach, migration data-copy, and the fleet
  SSH-health sweep. Two places already did this correctly (`worker/index.ts:712,814`,
  `worker/game-subdomain-sync.ts`) and prove the fix pattern; `worker/volumes.ts`/`worker/disk-expand.ts`
  already select the `node` relation for their Proxmox calls and self-heal for free once the root
  function is fixed — a genuinely mechanical, no-new-infrastructure fix once identified.
- **A separate class of bug needs real new infrastructure, not just a code fix**: `worker/network.ts`'s
  NAT/DNAT sync, `worker/index.ts`'s cloud-init snippet write, and `lib/dedicated-ip.ts`'s DNAT
  double-allocation check all shell out to the *local* machine's iptables/filesystem — since there is
  exactly one worker process for the whole platform and it runs only on the primary, none of these can
  ever reach a second physical node's kernel/disk without either SSH-to-node (a deliberate departure
  from this codebase's existing "every host reached via a scoped API token, never raw SSH" posture for
  Proxmox nodes) or a small per-node agent with its own bearer token (chosen — see the reference section
  below).
- **A live, if narrow, security exposure**: `scripts/onboard-node.sh` never installed the primary's own
  proven firewall-hardening system (`nxeon-firewall.service` + `fail2ban`, both real and running on the
  primary since 2026-07-26) onto a new node — `node-2` had zero admin-IP allowlisting from the moment it
  came online, confirmed via `nft list tables` returning nothing. Fixed same-day (ported + adapted for
  a pure-compute-node's stricter posture: `node-2` allowlists **both** tcp/22 and tcp/8006, unlike the
  primary, which deliberately leaves 22 open as a recovery channel for its own public web app — see
  `scripts/firewall.nft`'s header for the full reasoning either way). Confirmed live and working within
  seconds of applying: a real unauthorized packet was dropped by the new ruleset before the apply script
  even finished its own preflight window.
- A few smaller, independent findings: `lib/monitoring.ts`'s `backupSummary()` merges every node's
  backup listing into one scalar, so a healthy primary backup masks a silently-broken node-2 schedule
  forever; the admin disaster-recovery panel (`lib/platform-backups.ts`) and the customer backup-download
  route both only ever look at the primary's local disk; and four `Server` rows had `nodeId: null`
  (three genuinely live on the primary and backfilled directly; one — an old suspended test Minecraft
  server whose VM had actually been destroyed weeks earlier during the 2026-08-21 RAM-tuning cleanup,
  never properly deleted from the DB — removed outright once confirmed harmless).

See the "Multi-node synergy" reference section below for the resulting architecture decisions and the
staged plan; check `git log`/this file's future entries for what has actually shipped versus what is
still planned, since this rollout is explicitly being executed and documented phase-by-phase rather than
all at once.

### Lessons for node #3 and beyond

- **A second node changes the risk class of bugs that were merely latent with one node.** Several of
  the issues above (the vmid-collision risk on `nodeId: null` rows, the SSH-target bug) existed in the
  code for a long time without ever mattering, because "the primary" and "the only node" were the same
  machine. Adding a node doesn't introduce these bugs — it activates them. Treat "we're adding a second
  node" as a trigger to specifically re-audit anything that was ever written assuming a singular node,
  not just to test that the new node's own happy path works.
- **Verify infrastructure claims against the live system, don't infer them.** This rollout's own
  mistakes were caught by checking live state instead of trusting an assumption: the primary's real

```
Pass `--nvme-zpool <poolname>` on the initial run to skip this manual step going forward, if the
pool name is known ahead of time.

**`firewall-safe-apply.sh`'s default `REQUIRED_PORTS="22 80 443"` false-positives on a pure-compute
node.** That default is tuned for the *primary's own* public web app; a compute-only node (confirmed
against node-2's own live, weeks-old, healthy ruleset — zero 80/443 rules, drop policy) only genuinely
needs 22. Override via `NXEON_FW_REQUIRED_PORTS='22'`, and remember it must be passed to **both** the
`--check` and the `--apply` invocation separately — each `ssh host "..."` call is a fresh shell, so an
env var set for `--check` does not carry over to a later `--apply` call in the same session.

**A cosmetic-but-confusing systemd bookkeeping gap.** `firewall-safe-apply.sh` applies the ruleset via
a direct `nft -f`, never `systemctl start nxeon-firewall` — so even after a fully successful,
`--confirm`-ed apply, the service unit itself can still read `ActiveState=inactive`/`SubState=dead`
(with `Result=success`, since nothing ever failed) even though the real kernel ruleset is live and
correct. `WantedBy=multi-user.target` still means it runs correctly on the next real boot regardless,
but the mismatched status is confusing to read later. Run `systemctl start nxeon-firewall` once after
confirming the apply — same idempotent ruleset, just brings the unit's tracked state in line with
`ActiveState=active`/`SubState=exited`, matching node-2's own long-running state.

**Backup storage needs a real decision on hardware without a dedicated second disk.** `Node.storageHdd`
defaults to `vmdata-hdd`, a Proxmox `dir` storage at `/tank/backup` — on primary and node-2 this is
backed by a real, separate spinning disk (3.6TB and 1.7TB respectively). SYS-1 has no third disk: both
NVMe drives are fully consumed by the `vmdata` ZFS mirror, so `/tank/backup` silently resolved to a
directory on the 20GB OS root partition — not a real backup volume, and the admin dashboard's BACKUP
dimension read this correctly as broken ("no backups found," effectively a phantom storage) once a
customer actually landed there. Fixed by carving a sibling dataset out of the *same* pool already
backing `vmdata` (which had 884GB genuinely free — only OS templates lived there):
```
zfs create -o mountpoint=/tank/backup data/backup
mkdir -p /tank/backup/dump /tank/backup/snippets /tank/backup/template/{iso,cache}
```
No `storage.cfg`/DB change needed — `vmdata-hdd` already pointed at that exact path, it just had
nothing real behind it. This matches how primary and node-2 already share one pool between VM images
and backups with no quota split, relying on the platform's existing disk-utilization alerting rather
than a hard-partitioned reservation. **Check for a genuine second/third disk before onboarding any
future node that isn't a KS-3-class box** — if there truly isn't one, carving a same-pool dataset like
this is the correct default, not a workaround; a real separate physical disk (add-on, or object
storage) is a cost/reliability decision for the business, not something to assume is present.

**Verification performed, matching the runbook's step 5 bar exactly**: `testNode()`'s own checks
replicated directly (Proxmox `/status` reachable, node-agent `/v1/health` OK), all 10 OS templates
present and confirmed `template: 1`, a real throwaway server provisioned and reached with a genuine
external SSH connection **from node-2** (a truly separate host on a different provider, not just the
primary) — proving the NAT hop works from an arbitrary point on the public internet, not merely from
the one host most likely to already have a working route. Server destroyed via a real `DELETE` job
(not manual cleanup) afterward; `node-3.enabled` flipped to `true` only once all of the above was
confirmed, and confirmed live afterward that `scheduleNode()` — the real auto-picker both VPS and
game orders go through — genuinely considers it (an empty node sorts first by free RAM, so it will
be preferred over the primary/node-2 until it fills toward their level).

## Multi-node synergy — how it works, and how to add node N

This is the standing reference for the architecture described above; update it as further phases of the
2026-09-05 rollout land; each phase should update this section in the same commit as its code, not after.

### The `Node` model, at a glance

One row per physical Proxmox host: `apiUrl`/`tokenId`/`tokenSecret` (a scoped Proxmox API token — every
======
### Adding node N — the runbook

1. **Physical/VM setup**: check the provider's own server configurator for a native Proxmox VE
   template first (OVH offers one directly in its install wizard — used for node-3 and node-4, simpler
   than the alternative below). If none exists, install via the provider's rescue tooling +
   `proxmox-auto-install-assistant`; see the "physical install" section above for the exact
   QEMU-rescue-mode technique and its two gotchas. Either way, match the primary's PVE version where
   possible, and pick a **fresh `--node-num`** that doesn't collide with any existing node's subnet/NAT
   chain (check `/admin/nodes` for what's already assigned — node-3 deliberately used 3, not 2, to
   avoid node-2's `10.20.1.0/24`/`NXEON_FWD_N2`; node-4 used 4).
   **The kit (`scripts/onboard-node.sh` + its prerequisite files) must NOT be copied to the exact same
   path it installs to** (`/opt/nxeon/scripts/`) — step 9's `install` call refuses to copy a file onto
   itself and aborts the whole script under `set -e`. Hit for real onboarding node #4; fixed in the
   script itself (compares resolved paths first) but worth knowing if running an older checkout.
   **The OVH install wizard's own SSH-key field only grants YOUR key** — the primary still needs its own
   key (`/root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub`) appended to the new node's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` by hand (from a
   session using your key) before any of this can be run from the primary. If primary's earlier failed
   auth attempts (e.g. while sorting out key propagation) trip the freshly-installed fail2ban jail, the
   node becomes briefly unreachable from primary specifically — `fail2ban-client status sshd` from a
   still-working session confirms it, `fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip <primary-ip>` clears it.
2. **Check the disk layout before anything else** — specifically, whether this box has a genuine
   second/third disk separate from the NVMe pair `vmdata` will consume, the way primary and node-2 (both
   KS-3-class) do. If not (confirmed on SYS-1: 2x NVMe only, both go into one ZFS mirror), `vmdata-hdd`'s
   default path will silently resolve to a directory on the small OS root partition instead of a real
   backup volume — plan to carve a same-pool dataset for it in step 3 rather than discovering this only
   once a customer's backup goes missing. See the node-3 retrospective above for the exact commands.
3. **Firewall, before anything else is network-reachable**: copy `scripts/firewall-node.nft` (the
   permanent, generalized template — do NOT hand-adapt the primary's `scripts/firewall.nft` again),
   `admin-ip.sh`, `firewall-safe-apply.sh`, `firewall-reachability.sh`, `deploy/nxeon-firewall.service`,
   and `deploy/fail2ban-nxeon.jail.conf`. `scripts/onboard-node.sh`'s own step 7 now does this part of
   the work automatically (seeds `/etc/nxeon/admin-ips.nft` and `/etc/nxeon/agent-allow.nft` with the
   primary's IP, writes a genuine `/etc/nxeon/firewall.nft.rollback` reflecting this host's real prior
   state, installs everything) — it deliberately stops short of applying it. Apply yourself via
   `firewall-safe-apply.sh`'s full check/apply/verify-from-a-fresh-connection/confirm flow — never a raw
   `nft -f` — and when verifying, don't just prove your OWN connection still works: also confirm an
   unrelated/unlisted source is genuinely still refused on the admin ports (`nft list ruleset` directly,
   or a real second source), and that a "successful" `--rollback` actually removed everything you expect
   by re-listing the ruleset afterward. Both of those specific things were the actual bugs a same-source
   check missed live on node-2 — see the Phase 3 writeup above. **A pure-compute node needs only port 22
   — pass `NXEON_FW_REQUIRED_PORTS='22'` to override the script's `22 80 443` default (tuned for the
   primary's own public web app), and pass it to BOTH the `--check` and the `--apply` invocation
   separately (each is a fresh SSH session; the env var does not carry over).** After a confirmed apply,
   run `systemctl start nxeon-firewall` once — the apply itself uses a direct `nft -f`, so the unit's own
   `ActiveState` otherwise stays misleadingly `inactive` despite the ruleset being genuinely live; this
   is cosmetic, not a real gap, but confusing to read later if skipped.
4. **`scripts/onboard-node.sh`**: 10 steps — NAT bridge, storages, cloud-init snippet dir, Proxmox API
   role/user/token, templates (prefer copying from the primary via `vzdump`/`qmrestore` over
   `--build-templates`, so nodes serve byte-identical images), the firewall (previous item), the
   node-agent (installs Node.js if missing, generates a TLS cert + bearer token, installs the systemd
   unit), and local disaster-recovery backups (installs `backup-vms.sh`/`backup-pve-config.sh` +
   `nxeon-backup-vms.timer`, runs an immediate first pass — see "Multi-node disaster-recovery backups"
   above). Needs `--primary-ip` for the firewall/agent steps; `--skip-firewall`/`--skip-agent`/
   `--skip-backups` opt out of each independently. **`vmdata` storage is not auto-created unless you pass `--nvme-zpool
   <poolname>`** — the script only warns otherwise. If skipped, find the real pool name
   (`zpool list`/`zpool status` — do not guess) and register it manually:
   `pvesm add zfspool vmdata --pool <poolname> --content images,rootdir --sparse 1`. If step 2 found no
   separate backup disk, also carve the backup dataset now (see the node-3 retrospective above).
5. **Register in `/admin/nodes/new`** with the values the script prints, including the new Agent
   port/token fields, plus Provider/Region. Run `testNode()` — it now probes the node-agent's health
   endpoint too, alongside the Proxmox API check. Leave `enabled: false` until verified end-to-end.
6. **Verify with a real throwaway test server** provisioned on the new node before enabling it for real
   customer traffic: web terminal, file manager, game console (if applicable), backups, and the fleet
   SSH-health sweep should all work against it with no false alarms, AND (now that the node-agent
   exists) a genuine external SSH connection to its NAT-forwarded port should succeed from a real
   separate host — not just a guest-agent ping, and not necessarily the primary either (node-3 was
   verified from node-2, a host on a genuinely different provider, which is a stronger proof the NAT hop
   works from an arbitrary point on the public internet). A guest-agent ping alone proves the guest
   booted and cloud-init ran; it does NOT prove the NAT hop exists, and treating it as sufficient was
   exactly the mistake the Phase 1 writeup above documents. Tear the test server down through a real
   `DELETE` job (not manual `qm destroy` + manual row cleanup) so it exercises the same teardown path a
   real customer cancellation uses. Only then flip `enabled: true` — and it's worth confirming
   afterward that `scheduleNode()` actually considers the new node (an empty node sorts first by free
   RAM, so a freshly enabled node is typically *preferred* for the next several orders, not just
   eligible for them).

### Known limitations (as of 2026-09-05)

- No cross-node private VM networking (see NAT-island principle above) — not needed for independent
  single-node VPS/game hosting, would need a WireGuard/VXLAN overlay if a future feature requires it.
- No automated template-drift detection between nodes — parity is currently a onboarding-time discipline
  (copy, don't rebuild), not an enforced/verified invariant. (This already bit node-2 once — see the
  Phase 1 writeup above: its templates' `cicustom` pointed at a storage name that only existed on the
  primary.)
- The node-agent's `backup`-related endpoints (streaming a node's own backup archives, per-node
  disaster-recovery status) are a later extension of the same agent, not shipped with its first version
  (Phase 4).
- **RESOLVED (Phase 3, 2026-09-05)**: a non-primary node can now serve NAT-based (non-dedicated-IP)
  traffic — verified with a real external SSH connection to a real throwaway server on node-2, not just
  a guest-agent ping. Guest-level health (cloud-init, guest-agent, password SSH) and customer-level
  reachability (the NAT hop) remain two
  independent things — a node can be fully correct on the first and still totally unreachable on the
  second. Do not treat a healthy guest-agent ping as proof a node is ready for real NAT-based orders.
